newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU committee discusses French, German EMU plans.
newsitem.headline: EU committee discusses French, German EMU plans.

text.p: The European Union's monetary committee was meeting on Wednesday to discuss French and German economic convergence programmes to qualify for the European single currency, monetary officials said.

The panel of senior treasury and central bank officials was also to continue work on a second European Exchange Rate Mechanism, known as ERM II, to link national currencies that fail to meet the single currency requirements, or do not wish to take part in monetary union from the start in 1999.
It was also expected to provide orientations on a system of fines to punish countries running excessive deficits after the single currency, the euro, has been introduced.

France and Germany have recently submitted fresh convergence programmes outlining their efforts to meet the criteria for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU). The move follows a request from the European Commission, which judged their existing plans along with those of Italy, Belgium and Portugal were "outdated".
The new plans mainly incorporate already announced budgetary measures for 1997 and economic forecasts for the following years, one national monetary source said.

It is unclear how far they stretch, but the source admitted they may go beyond 1999 because of the need to assess national capitals' long-term commitment to sound finances as requested in the bloc's stability pact for the euro agreed last December in Dublin.
Some existing programmes end in 1997, the year when EU countries' economic performance will be judged to decide whether they are fit for the euro.
The French and German convergence plans are set to be discussed by EU finance ministers at their next scheduled meeting on March 17.
France is expecting to cut its budget deficit to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product in 1997 and 2.8 percent in 1998 from 4.0 percent in 1996.

Germany is also determined to slash its deficit to 2.9 percent in 1997 from 3.9 percent in 1996, but many economists see it clearly over the three-percent threshold set in the Maastricht treaty on EMU.
In February, the ministers gave their blessing to Belgium's revised plan for the period 1997-2000. Portugal and Italy are still expected to present theirs to the Commission.
Other items on the agenda of the regular meeting of the monetary committee include technical characteristics of euro coins and the assessment of national central banks' legal statute.

The Maastricht treaty says that central banks must be independent from the political power, a requirement which is not met by all and most notably by the Bank of England. -- Brussels Newsroom 32 2 287 6800
